parts.t: RECIPE 17 — Free slide decks with NotebookLM
From: How I created these VIRAL POWERPOINTS (free with ai) · 13 Dec 2025 · 11:38 · watch
You give NotebookLM some sources and a design prompt. It builds a slide deck from those sources in a few minutes, for free. The prompt mostly changes the look.
Only the beginner prompt is read out, and even that one stops before its theme.
THE ONE THING — the sources decide what the deck says
A notebook is a workspace. You add sources first, and the deck is built from them.
"Think of sources as the information that notebook LM is going to use to craft your PowerPoint presentation." (01:30)
Sources can be a YouTube link, a website, a Google Drive file or pasted text (01:30). She also mixes in audio files (03:31). There is a web search to find more (02:01).
Her last point is the one to keep:
"viral presentations are not necessarily visually loud. They are intellectually loud" (11:00)
Why this matters to you
You already have written research: rankings, buyer notes, what each binder contains. That is exactly the kind of text a notebook takes as a source.
The tool turns it into something you can look at in pages, not paragraphs.
The design prompt is not where the facts come from. If the source is thin, the deck will be thin, however good the prompt.
The steps she shows
Go to NotebookLM and click "try Notebook LM". She says to sign up "completely for free. Just use a personal Gmail account." (01:01)
Click "create new notebook" (01:01).
Add a source. Her demo used one of her own YouTube videos: click YouTube, paste the link, click insert (01:30).
On the right, find the slide deck button and click its pencil icon (02:31).
The default is a detailed deck. She picks a shorter length so it generates faster (02:31).
Paste the prompt into "describe the slide deck you want to create". You can add your own outline there too, but "this is optional" (03:00).
Click generate. It takes "a couple minutes" per deck, and you can start the next one while it runs (03:31).
When it is done, the preview has buttons to rename, share, show the prompt used, download as a PDF, and start a slideshow (07:31).
The three prompt levels — what is actually shown
Beginner — read out, but not all of it
The words she speaks at 02:31 are:
"You are a top.1% PowerPoint presentation designer using only the provided sources. Create a visually stunning viral slide deck"
She then lists the principles: "Visuals first, one main idea per slide, minimal text, and here's the theme."
That is the caption as heard. "top.1%" is probably "top 0.1%". Her theme text is on screen but never spoken, so it is not in the transcript. Do not treat the quote above as the full prompt.
Intermediate — described, not read
She says it adds guidance on visuals, "particularly one strong visual metaphor for each slide", plus a narrative and story arc (04:01).
Advanced — described, not read
She says it builds on the intermediate one and adds (05:00, 05:31, 06:01):
a longer list of "viral visual layouts"
turning data into "clean, elegant visualizations"
a content order: a strong start, the context, the central concept, key components
typography and theme rules you can change to your own colours
safety rules at the bottom
The safety rules tell it to use only ideas "explicitly present in the sources". She says this "helps reduce hallucinations" (06:30).
The full intermediate and advanced prompts are not in this recipe. She points to two places for them:
her newsletter, linked in the video description (04:01)
her shared notebook, which she calls "publicly available" (11:00), and where you can "copy paste the prompts directly" (07:00)
Her other route is to screenshot the prompt from the video and have ChatGPT type it out (04:01). That is a copy made by a model reading an image. Check it word for word before you rely on it.
Her own verdict on the three
This is one demo, one source and her own eye. It is not a test.
Before any of this goes near a listing
The deck is made of AI graphics, not your pages. Nothing in the video puts a real product page into a slide. A listing image must show what the buyer actually gets.
A slide with an invented binder picture would misrepresent the product.
Safer uses first. A private deck of your own research. A buyer guide slide that explains, in words, what is inside a binder, checked line by line against the real PDF.
AI disclosure on Etsy. The video says nothing about it. Check Etsy's current rules yourself before any NotebookLM slide goes into a listing or a download.
Your rule on artwork. It bans code-drawn art as product art. These are AI-made graphics, a different thing, but the same worry applies: nobody checked what the picture shows.
Facts can still drift. Even the advanced prompt only "helps reduce" hallucinations. Read every number on every slide against its source.
Sharing is public. She shares her notebook with a public link. Sharing yours, or posting a deck, is a public step and needs your yes.
Price. The only price in the video is "free", as of 13 Dec 2025. Uploading your notes also puts them in a Google account.
What to try — one step, tonight
This costs nothing and makes nothing public.
Step 5 is the point. Count how many slides say something your note does not. That number tells you whether this is safe to use for buyers.
ALSO MENTIONED
She calls NotebookLM "the best underrated free AI tool" (01:01).
If you already have an outline, paste it first and put the design prompt below it (10:32).
For social sharing, "simpler colors and less detailed graphics work well" (09:00). Her opinion, no figures shown.
Her opening claim: a deck "in 5 minutes" (00:00). Her own demo says a couple of minutes per deck, after sources and prompt.
Her intro: she "built and sold an AI company for millions of dollars" (00:30).
See also
RECIPE 04, the grader pattern: step 5 above is a grader, done by you. RECIPE 13, Claude and Canva templates: another route to visuals, where you control the layout.
RECIPE 05, the audience playbook: what the deck should say matters more than how it looks, which is her closing point too.
